<reflection>
After two experiments, the fitting results show that many mechanisms have very similar negative log-likelihoods, with M4 currently the best but closely followed by M7, M11, M14, M20, etc. The differences among the top mechanisms are small (within ~1.7 NLL units), indicating that the data so far does not strongly discriminate among them. The two experiments varied catalyst concentration (0.05 and 0.1) at fixed high substrate (2.0) and no product. This provided information on catalyst dependence but left substrate dependence and product effects unexplored. The aim of the second experiment was to probe catalyst dependence, which was achieved, but further discrimination is needed.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the top candidate mechanisms, we need to introduce a new experimental dimension: the effect of product. Many mechanisms involve product inhibition, product-induced deactivation, or reversible product formation (e.g., M12, M17, and most reversible mechanisms). By adding an initial concentration of product, we can observe how the reaction kinetics change compared to the product-free runs. This will help distinguish mechanisms that are sensitive to product concentration from those that are not. Specifically, mechanisms with product deactivation (M12, M17) may show reduced initial rates or altered progress curves, while reversible mechanisms (M1, M2, etc.) may show equilibrium shifts. We choose moderate conditions: substrate=2.0 (same as previous runs for comparison), catalyst=0.05 (same as run1), and product=0.2 (within allowed range, not extreme). This design avoids saturation or depletion and allows direct comparison with run1 to isolate the product effect. It is effective because it targets a wide range of mechanisms simultaneously, particularly those with product-related steps, without favoring a single pair.
</hypothesis>
